title: My Eyes Can Trick Me!
objective: Students will understand that their eyes and brain can sometimes see things differently than they actually are, and that it’s okay to check and ask questions.
materials: Large printout of the duck/rabbit illusion
Two identical colors of construction paper in different contexts (one surrounded by dark paper, one by light paper)
**Recommended from Perception Lab:** Rubin’s Vase (#4 — faces or vase?)
connection: **Option 1 — Visit the Mini Museum:** *“When you visit the Mini Museum, you’ll see old toys that tricked people’s eyes over 100 years ago! You’ll see a special old camera called a stereoscope that makes flat pictures look 3D, and cards that change when you move them.”*

**Option 2 — Virtual Visit:** Show the exhibition online at minimuseumproject.org/exhibitions/seeing-is-deceiving or view individual artifacts at minimuseumproject.org/exhibitions/seeing-is-deceiving/artifacts

steps.title: Our eyes are amazing
script: *“Today we’re going to learn that our eyes are amazing, but sometimes they play tricks on us! Has anyone ever thought they saw something, but it turned out to be something different?”*

Share a personal, age-appropriate story. Example: *“One time I thought I saw my friend across the street and I waved, but when I got closer, it was someone else who just looked like my friend from far away!”*

screen.question: Has anyone ever thought they saw something, but it turned out to be something different?

steps.purpose: Start from the children’s own times when their eyes played a trick.
students: Our eyes are amazing, but sometimes they play tricks on us!

steps.title: Duck or rabbit?
script: **Introduce the duck/rabbit:** Show the picture. *“Is this a duck or a rabbit?”* [Let students share what they see first.] *“It’s both! Your brain can see it two different ways. That’s called an optical illusion—when your eyes trick you.”*

screen.question: Is this a duck or a rabbit?

steps.purpose: Meet a first optical illusion: one picture the brain can see two ways.

steps.title: Faces or vase?
script: For each: *“What do you see first? Can you see it a different way?”*

screen.alt: Rubin’s Vase: a white vase on black, or two dark faces looking at each other
screen.caption: Rubin’s Vase

steps.purpose: Look at one illusion together, and let every child say what they see.
students: Can you see it a different way?

steps.title: Both are right!
script: Celebrate all answers: *“Great! Some people see it one way, some see it another way. Both are right!”*

items.label: A vase
items.alt: Rubin’s Vase with the vase picked out

items.label: Two faces
items.alt: Rubin’s Vase with the two faces picked out

steps.purpose: Celebrate every answer: the same picture can be seen two ways.
students: Some people see it one way, some see it another way. Both are right!

steps.title: Same or different?
script: Show two pieces of identical construction paper surrounded by different colored backgrounds
*“Are these the same color or different colors?”* Take predictions

screen.question: Are these the same color or different colors?

steps.title: Side by side
script: Put them side by side to reveal they’re identical
*“See? What’s around them changed how they looked! Your eyes got tricked by what was next to the colors.”*
*“It’s okay if you weren’t sure! Our eyes can trick us sometimes. That’s why it’s always good to look closer and check.”*

screen.question: It’s okay if you weren’t sure! Our eyes can trick us sometimes. That’s why it’s always good to look closer and check.

steps.purpose: Reveal that the colors are the same, and make it safe to have been fooled.
students: What’s around them changed how they looked!

steps.title: Before we decide
script: *“Sometimes we might think a friend is mad at us because of how their face looks, but maybe they’re just tired or thinking hard. Before we decide how someone feels, we should ask them! Just like checking if the colors are really the same.”*
“If you think someone took your toy, check first—maybe it’s just in a different spot”
“If you think someone isn’t being nice, ask them what they meant before getting upset”
“If something looks scary from far away, get closer to see what it really is”

screen.question: Before we decide how someone feels, we should ask them!

steps.purpose: Carry “check first” from pictures into friendships and everyday life.
students: “If you think someone took your toy, check first—maybe it’s just in a different spot”
“If you think someone isn’t being nice, ask them what they meant before getting upset”
“If something looks scary from far away, get closer to see what it really is”

steps.title: Look closer and ask
script: *“Remember: It’s always okay to look closer and ask questions. Even grown-ups’ eyes play tricks on them sometimes!”*
**Exit question:** *“If your friend sees something different than you, what should you do?”* (Look again! / Ask questions! / Both can be right!)

screen.question: If your friend sees something different than you, what should you do?

steps.purpose: The exit question: what to do when we see things differently.
